newsitem.title: UK: FTSE's fate hangs on Greenspan, politics next week.
newsitem.headline: FTSE's fate hangs on Greenspan, politics next week.

text.p: The fate of London's FTSE share index hangs on Alan Greenspan next week, and the Federal Reserve chairman has the power to inspire a charge to new peaks or a tumble back from recent highs, analysts said on Friday.

Greenspan delivers his Humphrey Hawkins testimony on the U.S. economic outlook on Wednesday and Thursday. Analysts said a benign speech could fire up markets across the globe and spur more record-breaking climbs by both the FTSE and the Dow.
But hints of higher rates or a repeat of his warning against "irrational exuberance" could send stock markets sliding.

"Humphrey Hawkins will definitely be the key focus for world markets," said Robert Buckland, UK strategist at HSBC James Capel. "We'll be looking for indicators from him about whether he's going to tighten rates. But for the time being the markets are pretty happy with the outlook for U.S. interest rates."
David Aserkoff, strategist at Credit Suisse First Boston, said he expected Greenspan to paint a benign picture.

"Greenspan will probably tell us that economic growth was quite strong in the second half, which we knew, but that it is slowing into relatively benign levels in the first half of this year," Aserkoff said.

"He'll say he likes the low inflation, steady growth mix, and that obviously the Fed will be watching for signs of inflation but the atmosphere is relatively healthy," Aserkoff said. But he warned markets might find it difficult to advance even if Greenspan's speech boosted Wall Street.

"It would provide a relief bounce but that may prompt some profit-taking," Aserkoff said. "It's got to be hard for portfolio managers to be sitting on this many gains this early and not feel tempted to take a bit of money off the table."

Analysts said there was little data to chew on next week. Instead, the main domestic influences on the FTSE would be a flood of blue-chip results and the Wirral South by-election on Thursday, they said.

A British general election is due by May 22 and the by-election will provide a gauge of opinion. The main opposition Labour Party, which is ahead of the ruling Conservatives in national opinion polls, is expected to win the seat from the Conservatives.
Analysts said the market was discounting a Labour general election win and a Labour victory in the by-election would not have a major impact on the FTSE.
But a surprise Conservative win could rattle the FTSE, despite the traditional preference among analysts for the party.
"If the Conservatives win the Wirral that would raise the spectre of a hung parliament," Buckland said.

"The worst scenario for the market is the one in the middle. The market can live with the Labour majority that everyone is expecting; it would probably prefer a Conservative majority, but what it doesn't want is something in-between," he said.
"There would be worries about how monetary policy would be set in such a scenario, and the prospect of another election within a short time. It would all start to get much messier."
On the corporate results front, Monday sees first-quarter figures from Hanson Plc.
On Tuesday, full-year results are due from Guardian Royal Exchange Plc, National Westminster Bank Plc, Sema Group Plc, and EMI Group Plc releases nine-month results and trading statement.
British Aerospace Plc, Commercial Union Plc and Prudential Corp Plc report annual results on Wednesday, and LASMO Plc and the now-demerged British Gas announce annual figures on Thursday.
